summary: In some inter-AS and inter-area setups, a router replying to an LSP Ping from RFC 4379 may have no route back to the initiator, so the reply is dropped and the test falsely fails. This standards-track RFC adds a relayed echo reply mechanism that passes the reply along through another router. It updates RFC 4379.

eli5.summary: If you cannot reach someone directly, you give your answer to a friend who knows the way. That friend carries the reply back to the person who asked.

subtitle: Lets a router with no route back to the pinger hand its LSP Ping reply to relay nodes that can deliver it.

tldr.problem: In inter-AS and inter-area networks, a router answering an LSP Ping often has no route to the initiator, so its Echo Reply is discarded and the test falsely fails.
tldr.mechanism: A new Relayed Echo Reply message and a Relay Node Address Stack TLV let the replying router pass its reply through a chain of routable relay nodes, such as ASBRs, until it reaches the initiator.
tldr.outcome: Ping and traceroute work across address domains. The RFC updates RFC 4379 and is a Standards Track document.

facts.label: Relay Node Address Stack TLV type

today: RFC 7743 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2016. It updates RFC 4379 and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why Echo Replies Get Lost
sections.content:
RFC 4379 defines LSP Ping to find data-plane failures. The Echo Reply goes back as a UDP packet addressed to the LSR that sent the Echo Request. That works only if every LSR can route back to the originator. In practice, intra-provider routing policy, route hiding and network address translation at ASBRs often prevent it. In inter-AS cases, the only node in one AS that the other AS may route to directly is usually the ASBR.

The RFC gives two examples. In a simple inter-AS LSP from PE1 to PE2, P2 in AS2 cannot send a reply to PE1 because PE1's address is routable in AS1 but not in AS2. In a seamless MPLS design, core LSRs have no IP route to the access nodes. Either way the initiator sees a path break and cannot localize the fault.

The fix is to let a relay node, for example an ASBR, forward the message. Each relay node must be reachable by the next one, and the chain can be followed recursively until the initiator is reached. The mechanism is defined for unicast only, and for a path that uses a single address family throughout.
sections.eli5: A helper far away has no way to call you directly, so the answer is lost. This fixes it by letting helpers on the way pass the answer along.

sections.title: The Relayed Echo Reply Message
sections.content:
The RFC adds a third message type next to Echo Request and Echo Reply: MPLS Relayed Echo Reply, Message Type value 5. It is a UDP packet whose payload has the same format as an Echo Request or Reply, and it uses the same UDP port 3503 as the rest of LSP Ping. It is used in place of the Echo Reply when the replying LSR is sending to a relay node rather than to the initiator.

A second addition is the return code 20, 'One or more TLVs not returned due to MTU size'. It tells the initiator that some TLVs were left out to keep the reply within the effective MTU. The RFC also updates step 7 of Section 4.4 of RFC 4379: if the best return code is 3 or 8 and the packet would exceed the MTU, the code becomes 20.
sections.eli5: There is now a special envelope for 'please pass this along.' It uses the same mailbox number as the normal reply envelope.

sections.title: The Relay Node Address Stack TLV
sections.content:
The optional Relay Node Address Stack TLV has Type 32768. It MUST be carried in the Echo Request, Echo Reply and Relayed Echo Reply messages whenever the relay mechanism is used. Its fixed part holds these fields:

  • Initiator Source Port: the UDP source port the initiator used, and where it expects the reply.
  • Reply Address Type: 0 (Null), 1 (IPv4) or 2 (IPv6), which sets the address length of 0, 4 or 16 octets.
  • Source Address of Replying Router: the address of whoever originated the reply.
  • Destination Address Offset: the offset from the top of stack to the destination entry.
  • Number of Relayed Addresses: how many entries the stack holds.

The stack of relayed addresses grows downward, so relay nodes further along the LSP appear lower. Each entry has an address type, a K bit and reserved fields, followed by the address. Entry sizes are 4 octets for Null, 8 for IPv4 and 20 for IPv6. If the K bit is 1, the entry MUST NOT be stripped during processing; it stays for the entire traceroute.
sections.eli5: The stack is a list of helper names written in order along the road. Some names have a 'keep me' sticker so they never get crossed off.

sections.title: Procedures for Requests and Relayed Replies
sections.content:
The initiator first discovers the relay nodes, then includes the TLV in its Echo Requests. In the first request the TLV MUST list the initiator's own address as the first entry, with the Destination Address Offset pointing at it and the replying-router address set to null. An LSR that does not recognize the TLV SHOULD ignore it, because its type is in the optional range.

A receiver of a request updates the replying-router address. It scans the stack from bottom to top for the last entry with the K bit set (or the top if none), then looks downward for the first routable address. That becomes the destination, and entries below it MUST be deleted. The receiver MUST then add at least one of its own addresses at the bottom, the last being reachable through the interface the request would have been forwarded to. A router configured to hide its address adds a NIL entry, and a node spanning two address domains, such as an ASBR, SHOULD set the K bit.

If the next relay node is not the first address in the list, the replying LSR SHOULD send a Relayed Echo Reply to it, with UDP ports both set to 3503. A relay node that receives one finds the next relay the same way and forwards it, with the TTL copied and decremented by 1. When the next node is the first entry, an Echo Reply is sent to the initiator, whose destination UDP port is copied from the Initiator Source Port field. During traceroute, the initiator SHOULD copy the stack from the previous Echo Reply into each next Echo Request. A NIL entry without the K bit MAY be removed, and one with the K bit MUST be removed if the traceroute continues.
sections.eli5: Each helper crosses off the names it cannot reach, adds its own name, and hands the answer to the nearest helper who can. The last helper gives it to the person who asked.

sections.title: Worked Example Across Two Autonomous Systems
sections.content:
The RFC walks through an LSP from PE1 to PE2 over the path PE1, P1, ASBR1, ASBR2, P2, PE2, where PE1 in AS1 is not reachable by P2 in AS2. PE1's first request has TTL=1 and carries only PE1's address. P1 adds its interface address facing ASBR1, without the K bit. When ASBR1 later sees the request, it deletes P1's address and adds its interface facing ASBR2 with the K bit set. ASBR2 adds its interface facing P2, also with the K bit set.

At TTL=4 the reply from P2 carries four addresses: PE1's, ASBR1's interface, ASBR2's interface and P2's interface facing PE2. P2 sends a Relayed Echo Reply to ASBR2, ASBR2 forwards it to ASBR1, and ASBR1 sends the final Echo Reply to PE1. TTL=5 follows the same path.

For traceroute display, the address printed is the Source Address of Replying Router from the TLV when it exists, otherwise the source IP address of the Echo Reply.
sections.eli5: The far helper hands its answer to the next helper, who hands it to the next, until the last one gives it to the person who asked.

sections.title: Security and Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
Putting a target router's address in the stack raises the risk of denial of service: such packets could overwhelm an LSR's control plane. A rate limiter SHOULD be applied to the well-known UDP port on the relay node, and a relay node SHOULD validate relayed replies against a set of valid source addresses and discard those from untrusted border routers. The stack also reveals path information, so the RFC recommends clearing the K bit unless it must be set and using NIL entries to hide node information. A receiver could check that the first stack address equals the source IP address in the request.

If a node on the LSP does not support the mechanism, it ignores the TLV. The initiator then may not get the TLV back from that node. An indication should be reported to the operator, and the next Echo Request should copy the TLV from the previous Echo Request. If that node sits between the initiator and the first relay node, the ping can continue without interruption.
sections.eli5: A list of helpers could be misused to flood a helper with junk, so helpers should only accept notes from people they trust, and hide names when they can.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content:
IANA assigned three values in the MPLS LSP Ping Parameters registry:

  • Message Type 5, 'MPLS Relayed Echo Reply', from the Standards Action range 0-191.
  • TLV Type 32768, 'Relay Node Address Stack TLV', from the Standards Action range 32768-49161.
  • Return Code 20, 'One or more TLVs not returned due to MTU size', from the range 0-191.
sections.eli5: The official number list now has entries for the new envelope, the new list of helpers, and the new 'some things did not fit' code.
